proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(\theta\in\Theta_S\).  Positivity in the definition of \(\Theta_S\) gives \(p_\theta(s)>0\) for every \(s\in S\).  For a supported fiber
\[
F_{\nu,t}=\{(a,z)\in S:z_{-\nu}=t\},\qquad |\nu|=\gamma,
\]
its probability is positive.  Hence the fortified conditional-mean-zero restriction is equivalent to
\[
0=\mathbb E_{P_\theta}\{d(A,Z)\mid Z_{-\nu}=t\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
0=\sum_{s\in F_{\nu,t}}p_\theta(s)d(s).
\]
Put \(q(s)=p_\theta(s)d(s)\).  The displayed restrictions are exactly the incidence equations in the specialization of \(H_S\) from \(x_s\) to \(p_\theta(s)\).  Coordinatewise division \(d(s)=q(s)/p_\theta(s)\) is valid by positivity, so multiplication by \(p_\theta\) is a bijection between the two spaces.

Likewise, if \(f\) is a function of \(C\), then
\[
[p_\theta f]_{a,b,c}=p_\theta(a,b,c)f(c)
=\sum_{c'}f(c')[r_{c'}(p_\theta)]_{a,b,c}.
\]
Thus multiplication maps \(L^2(C)\) onto \(R_S(p_\theta)\).  The supported \(c\)-sections are disjoint and their entries are positive, so the displayed spanning vectors are nonzero and every element of their span has the displayed form.

Write \(g_y=(g(v,a,c))_{v\in\mathcal U}\) for \(y=(a,c)\).  Using the factorization defining \(P_\theta\), for \(w=p_\theta(d+f)\in H_S+R_S(p_\theta)\) one has
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[(d(A,Z)+f(C))g(U,A,C)]
&=\sum_{(a,b,c)\in S}\sum_{v\in\mathcal U}
p_\theta(a,b,c)[\Pi_{\theta,(a,c)}]_{b,v}
(d(a,b,c)+f(c))g(v,a,c)\\
&=\left\langle w,\ \bigoplus_{y\in\mathcal I_S}\Pi_{\theta,y}g_y\right\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
The vector on the right gives the zero functional on all fortified supply vectors precisely when it lies in
\[
(H_S+R_S(p_\theta))^\perp=N_S(p_\theta).
\]
Therefore the kernel of \(\mathsf T_\theta\) is the kernel of the stated composite map to \(\mathbb R^S/N_S(p_\theta)\).  Two finite-dimensional linear maps with the same domain and the same kernel have the same rank, which proves the claim about \(M_\theta\).

Set
\[
V=\overline E_S/\overline N_S,\qquad d=|\mathcal D_S|,
\qquad \rho(I)=\dim_{\mathbb F_S}\left(\sum_{(y,j)\in I}W_y\right),
\qquad \delta=\eta(S).
\]
For an arbitrary choice \(w_e\in W_e\), where \(W_{(y,j)}=W_y\), and any \(I\subseteq\mathcal D_S\),
\[
\dim\operatorname{span}\{w_e:e\in\mathcal D_S\}
\le |\mathcal D_S\setminus I|+\rho(I)
=d-\{|I|-\rho(I)\}.
\]
Taking an \(I\) attaining the definition of \(\delta\) proves the upper bound \(d-\delta\).

For the reverse inequality, let \(T\) be a \(\delta\)-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb F_S\), and, in \(V\oplus T\), put \(W'_e=W_e\oplus T\).  For every nonempty \(I\), the definition of \(\delta\) gives
\[
\dim\left(\sum_{e\in I}W'_e\right)=\rho(I)+\delta\ge |I|;
\]
the empty-set inequality is automatic.  The cited linear independent-transversal theorem therefore supplies independent vectors \(w'_e=w_e+t_e\in W_e\oplus T\) for all \(e\in\mathcal D_S\).  Their span has dimension \(d\), while the kernel of its projection to \(V\) has dimension at most \(\dim T=\delta\).  Consequently
\[
\dim\operatorname{span}\{w_e:e\in\mathcal D_S\}\ge d-\delta.
\]
Together with the upper bound this proves that the maximum is \(d-\eta(S)\).

Choose bases of the \(\overline V_y\) and lift the vectors just constructed to those bases.  A \((d-\delta)\)-minor of the resulting coordinate matrix is nonzero.  Thus the arrays attaining the maximum contain the nonempty Zariski-open set on which this minor is nonzero; conversely, no larger minor can be nonzero by the preceding upper bound.  Since \(\mathbb F_S=\mathbb Q(x_s:s\in S)\) is infinite, successive avoidance of the finitely many roots at each coordinate produces a point of this open set with coordinates in \(\mathbb F_S\), which is the asserted rational-function representative.

It remains to verify the stochastic and positivity restrictions.  In each block choose a basis of \(\mathbb F_S^u\) whose first vector is \(\mathbf 1_u\).  A row-stochastic matrix sends this vector to \(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B_y}\); its other \(u-1\) images can be prescribed arbitrarily.  Modulo the constant image, those prescriptions range independently over \(\overline V_y\).  The uniform table sends all contrast basis vectors to zero.  Hence scaling the prescribed contrast images by a nonzero scalar does not change their span, and sufficiently small real scalings make every entry of the resulting row-stochastic tables strictly positive.

More explicitly, the nonzero minor above becomes a nonzero rational function of the \(x_s\) and of the contrast coordinates.  After clearing denominators it has a nonzero polynomial numerator with rational coefficients.  A nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on a nonempty Euclidean open set: this follows by induction on the number of variables, since a nonzero univariate polynomial has finitely many roots.  Therefore every sufficiently small neighborhood of the uniform tables, together with the positive orthant for the \(x_s\), contains a rational point where that numerator is nonzero.  Normalize the positive rational \(x_s\) to sum to one; common scaling does not change \(R_S(x)\), \(N_S(x)\), or rank.  This gives strictly positive rational row-stochastic blocks and proves the final realization assertion.

Let \(n=|\mathcal I_S|\) and \(d=n(u-1)=|\mathcal D_S|\).  By the weighted support reduction, rank is the dimension of the image of the block-column map modulo \(N_S(x)\).  In each row-stochastic block change the domain basis so that its first basis vector is \(\mathbf 1_u\).  The \(n\) first columns then span \(J_S\), whose image modulo \(N_S(x)\) has dimension
\[
\dim J_S-\dim(N_S(x)\cap J_S)=n-\kappa_0(S).
\]
After quotienting by that image, the remaining column indexed by \((y,j)\in\mathcal D_S\) ranges in
\[
(\overline V_y+\overline N_S)/\overline N_S=W_y.
\]
The product-block Rado theorem therefore gives the exact symbolic maximum
\[
(n-\kappa_0(S))+(d-\eta(S))
=un-\kappa_0(S)-\eta(S)
=Q_S-\kappa_0(S)-\eta(S). \tag{1}
\]

The realization part of that theorem supplies a positive rational specialization \(\theta_0\in\Theta_S\) at which a minor of order equal to the right side of (1) is nonzero.  Thus \(\operatorname{rank}M_{\theta_0}\) is at least that number.  No larger minor is nonzero over \(\mathbb F_S\), by (1).  If a larger minor were nonzero at some compatible numerical parameter, its determinant polynomial, restricted to the affine row-stochastic parameter space, would not be the zero polynomial, contradicting the symbolic maximum.  Hence equality holds at \(\theta_0\), and (1) is the generic rank.

Fix the nonzero maximal minor used above and clear its denominators.  Its nonvanishing locus inside \(\Theta_S\) is a nonempty relative Zariski-open set.  The parameter space is relatively open in the affine product of one probability simplex and the row-stochastic affine spaces.  By the elementary polynomial argument in the product-block proof, the zero set of a nonzero polynomial has empty relative interior and Lebesgue measure zero; the measure assertion follows by induction and Fubini from the corresponding univariate fact.  Its complement is therefore Euclidean dense and has full relative Lebesgue measure.  On that complement the selected minor is nonzero, while every larger minor vanishes identically, so the rank equals (1).

Finally, if \(\kappa_0(S)+\eta(S)>0\), equation (1) is strictly smaller than \(Q_S\).  Were \(\operatorname{rank}M_\theta=Q_S\) at any \(\theta\in\Theta_S\), some \(Q_S\)-minor would be nonzero there and hence would not vanish identically, again contradicting (1).  Thus the failure is uniform over all compatible positive parameters.

The generic-rank formula gives
\[
r_{\mathrm{gen}}(S)=Q_S-\kappa_0(S)-\eta(S).
\]
Both terms subtracted are nonnegative integers: \(\kappa_0(S)\) is a dimension, and \(\eta(S)\ge0\) because the empty set in its defining maximum has value zero.  Hence \(r_{\mathrm{gen}}(S)=Q_S\) if and only if both terms vanish.

For \(I\subseteq\mathcal D_S\), write
\[
\rho(I)=\dim_{\mathbb F_S}\left(\sum_{(y,j)\in I}W_y\right).
\]
By definition,
\[
\eta(S)=\max_{I\subseteq\mathcal D_S}\{|I|-\rho(I)\}.
\]
Since the maximum includes the value zero at \(I=\varnothing\), it is zero exactly when \(|I|-\rho(I)\le0\) for every \(I\), which is exactly the displayed family of Hall inequalities.  This proves both equivalences.

If either condition fails, the last part of the generic-rank theorem shows \(\operatorname{rank}M_\theta<Q_S\) at every \(\theta\in\Theta_S\).  This conclusion concerns only injectivity of the fortified pairing map.  The frozen assumptions contain neither a pair of observationally equivalent structural causal models with different \(\tau\) nor a completeness theorem asserting that this pairing condition is necessary for every possible identification route.  Therefore the proved implication is precisely law-uniform failure of this pairing route and does not logically imply nonidentification of \(\tau\).

For \(I\subseteq\mathcal D_S\), define
\[
\rho(I)=\mathcal O_S(I)
=\dim_{\mathbb F_S}\left(\sum_{(y,j)\in I}W_y\right),
\qquad F(I)=\rho(I)-|I|.
\]
The function \(\rho\) is submodular.  Indeed, with \(U_I=\sum_{e\in I}W_e\), the dimension identity and the inclusion \(U_{I\cap J}\subseteq U_I\cap U_J\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho(I)+\rho(J)
&=\dim(U_I+U_J)+\dim(U_I\cap U_J)\\
&\ge \dim U_{I\cup J}+\dim U_{I\cap J}
=\rho(I\cup J)+\rho(I\cap J).
\end{aligned}
\]
The modular function \(I\mapsto |I|\) satisfies equality in the same relation, so \(F=\rho-|\cdot|\) is submodular and integer-valued.  Apply the cited strongly polynomial submodular-minimization theorem to \(F\).  If \(I^*\) is the returned minimizer, then
\[
\eta(S)=\max_I\{|I|-\rho(I)\}=-\min_I F(I)=-F(I^*),
\]
so \(I^*\) is an exact maximizing deficient set.

It remains to compute the constant-direction defect.  From the matrices specified in the rank-oracle definition, exact Gaussian elimination over \(\mathbb F_S\) gives bases for \(H_S=\ker D_S\), \(R_S(x)\), \(L_S(x)=H_S+R_S(x)\), its annihilator \(N_S(x)\), and \(J_S\).  A second elimination yields
\[
\kappa_0(S)=\dim(N_S(x)\cap J_S)
=\dim N_S(x)+\dim J_S-\dim(N_S(x)+J_S).
\]
Finally the generic-rank formula returns
\[
r_{\mathrm{gen}}(S)=Q_S-\kappa_0(S)-\eta(S).
\]
Schrijver's algorithm makes polynomially many calls in \(|\mathcal D_S|\); all other displayed computations use polynomially many field operations on the finite input matrices.  By the definition of \(\mathcal O_S\), every oracle value and every auxiliary dimension is obtained by exact rational-function elimination.  Thus no floating-point specialization or probabilistic rank test enters the certificate.  The strong-polynomial assertion here is the stated oracle-call assertion; it does not assert a strongly polynomial bit-complexity bound for representing arbitrary rational functions.

Put \(b=m^\gamma\), \(c=m^{K-\gamma}\), and \(n=2c=|\mathcal I_S|\).  Then directly from the definition of \(Q_S\),
\[
Q_S=un=2u m^{K-\gamma}. \tag{2}
\]

We next compute the supply dimension.  In each coordinate write the \(m\)-dimensional function space as the direct sum of its constant line and an \((m-1)\)-dimensional contrast space.  The resulting tensor-interaction decomposition of functions of \(Z\) has, for each \(T\subseteq[K]\), an interaction summand of dimension \((m-1)^{|T|}\).  The row space of \(D_S\) consists of the treatment-constant functions whose interaction set \(T\) is contained in the complement of at least one \(\gamma\)-set.  Such a complement has size \(K-\gamma\), so this is equivalent to \(|T|\le K-\gamma\).  Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rank}D_S=\sum_{j=0}^{K-\gamma}\binom Kj(m-1)^j
\]
and, since \(|S|=2m^K\),
\[
\dim H_S
=2m^K-\sum_{j=0}^{K-\gamma}\binom Kj(m-1)^j
=m^K+\sum_{j=K-\gamma+1}^{K}\binom Kj(m-1)^j. \tag{3}
\]
The vectors \(r_c(x)\) have disjoint nonempty supports, so they are independent.  Moreover, if \(\sum_c\lambda_c r_c(x)\in H_S\), the incidence equation corresponding to \(\nu=\alpha\) and the fixed complement value \(c\) reads
\[
\lambda_c\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{b\in\prod_{i\in\alpha}\mathcal Z_i}x_{(a,b,c)}=0.
\]
The second factor is nonzero in \(\mathbb F_S\), hence \(\lambda_c=0\) for every \(c\).  Thus \(H_S\cap R_S(x)=\{0\}\), and (3) gives
\[
\dim L_S(x)=m^K+\sum_{j=K-\gamma+1}^{K}\binom Kj(m-1)^j+m^{K-\gamma}
=D_{K,m}(\gamma). \tag{4}
\]

For completeness, we now prove that the product-block restriction causes no further loss beyond the smaller of demand and (4).  We use the following elementary fiber-interpolation fact.  Let \(\mathcal G\) be the tensor-interaction space on \(B\times C\) spanned by interactions of order at most \(K-\gamma\), and put \(d_0=\dim\mathcal G\).  If \(1\le r\le b\), then for a nonempty Zariski-open set of block maps \(\Lambda_c:\mathbb F_S^b\to\mathbb F_S^r\),
\[
\operatorname{rank}\left((\Lambda_c)_c\bigm|_{\mathcal G}\right)=\min\{d_0,rc\}. \tag{5}
\]
Here is a direct verification of (5).  Use the constant-plus-contrast basis in every coordinate and order its tensor monomials first by the number of contrast factors and then lexicographically.  Process the \(C\)-cells lexicographically and, within a cell, process the \(r\) rows of \(\Lambda_c\).  Multivariate Newton elimination subtracts rows already pivoted on proper interaction subsets.  A new row then has its first nonzero coefficient on the first unpivoted interaction monomial; this continues until either all \(d_0\) monomials or all \(rc\) rows have pivots.  To see the induction explicitly, separating the last \(B\)-coordinate gives
\[
\mathcal G_{\gamma,q}
=\mathcal G_{\gamma-1,q}\otimes\langle\mathbf 1\rangle
\oplus\bigoplus_{k=1}^{m-1}\mathcal G_{\gamma-1,q-1}\otimes\langle e_k^0\rangle,
\qquad q=K-\gamma.
\]
Here \(\mathcal G_{\gamma-1,-1}=\{0\}\).  Row elimination first pivots the constant summand and then the \(m-1\) contrast summands; within each summand it is the same procedure with one fewer \(B\)-coordinate and, for a contrast summand, one less allowed interaction order.  The base case has no \(B\)-coordinate, where the functions of \(C\) supply the identity pivots.  Thus the pivot count satisfies
\[
\min\!\left\{rc,
\sum_{h=0}^{\min\{\gamma,q\}}\binom\gamma h(m-1)^h
\left(\sum_{j=0}^{q-h}\binom qj(m-1)^j\right)\right\}
=\min\{rc,d_0\},
\]
where the expression following \(rc\) is \(d_0\) by Vandermonde's identity.  Choosing the unused entries of the block maps successively outside the finitely many pivot zeros realizes these eliminations.  The corresponding maximal minor is therefore a nonzero polynomial, proving (5) on a nonempty Zariski-open set.

We apply (5) to the null space.  The orthogonal complement \(H_S^\perp\) is the treatment-constant copy of \(\mathcal G\), and
\[
d_0=\sum_{j=0}^{K-\gamma}\binom Kj(m-1)^j.
\]
Orthogonality to \(R_S(x)\) adds, independently for every \(c\), the equation
\[
\ell_c(g)=\sum_{a,b}x_{(a,b,c)}g(b,c)=0. \tag{6}
\]
These \(c\) equations are independent on \(\mathcal G\), because \(\mathcal G\) contains every function of \(C\).  Hence \(\dim N_S(x)=d_0-c\).  A vector in \(N_S(x)\cap J_S\) is independent of treatment, constant in \(b\), and so is a function only of \(c\); equation (6) then forces it to vanish.  Thus
\[
\kappa_0(S)=0. \tag{7}
\]

Let \(t=\min\{u,b\}\).  Choose generically in each block a \(t\)-dimensional column space \(P_{a,c}\) containing the constant vector.  For a fixed \(c\), two generic such spaces have intersection dimension
\[
s=\max\{1,2t-b\}.
\]
A vector of \(N_S(x)\) is treatment-constant, so membership in \(\bigoplus_{a,c}P_{a,c}\) requires its \(c\)-fiber to lie in \(P_{0,c}\cap P_{1,c}\).  Together with (6), these are
\[
r=b-s+1=\min\{b,2(b-t)+1\}
\]
generic block equations per \(c\).  Applying (5) gives
\[
\dim\left(N_S(x)\cap\bigoplus_{a,c}P_{a,c}\right)
=\max\{0,d_0-rc\}
=\max\{0,2ct-D_{K,m}(\gamma)\}. \tag{8}
\]
For the last equality, if \(2t\le b+1\), then \(r=b\), both sides are zero because \(d_0<m^K=bc\); if \(2t>b+1\), substitute \(r=2(b-t)+1\) and use \(D_{K,m}(\gamma)=2bc-d_0+c\), which follows from (3)--(4).

Thus the image of these block columns modulo \(N_S(x)\) has dimension
\[
2ct-\max\{0,2ct-D_{K,m}(\gamma)\}
=\min\{2ct,D_{K,m}(\gamma)\}. \tag{9}
\]
If \(u\le b\), then \(t=u\) and \(2ct=Q_S\).  If \(u>b\), then \(2ct=2bc=|S|\), while \(Q_S>|S|\ge D_{K,m}(\gamma)\).  In both cases (9) is \(\min\{Q_S,D_{K,m}(\gamma)\}\).  Every generic block space containing the constant vector is the column space of a row-stochastic table, and small perturbation of the uniform table makes it positive.  The generic-rank formula and (7)--(9) now yield
\[
Q_S-\kappa_0(S)-\eta(S)=\min\{Q_S,D_{K,m}(\gamma)\}.
\]
It equals \(Q_S\) exactly when \(D_{K,m}(\gamma)\ge Q_S\), proving the final frontier statement.

theorem.statement:
Assume \(\kappa_0(S)=\eta(S)=0\).  If \(u\ge2\), no such support has \(\operatorname{rank}M_\theta=Q_S\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta_S\).  Indeed, every such support admits a strictly positive compatible affine family \(\theta(t)\), defined for all sufficiently small positive and negative \(t\), for which \(\operatorname{rank}M_{\theta(0)}<Q_S\) and \(\operatorname{rank}M_{\theta(t)}=Q_S\) for every sufficiently small \(t\ne0\).

If \(u=1\), law-uniform full row rank holds if and only if there is no nonzero real vector \(j\in J_S\cap H_S^\perp\), with the orthogonal complement taken after base change of the incidence equations to \(\mathbb R\), having the following support-sign property: at every \(c\) supporting only one treatment level \(a\), \(j_{a,c}=0\); and at every \(c\) supporting both treatment levels, either \(j_{0,c}=j_{1,c}=0\) or \(j_{0,c}j_{1,c}<0\).  This is a finite exact sign-feasibility characterization determined by \(S\) and \(D_S\).  Whenever it fails, such a vector explicitly constructs a positive compatible affine family with the same crossing property.
theorem.proof_tex:
The generic-rank theorem and \(\kappa_0(S)=\eta(S)=0\) give a rational positive \(\theta_1\in\Theta_S\) with \(\operatorname{rank}M_{\theta_1}=Q_S\).

Suppose first that \(u\ge2\).  Keep \(p_{\theta_1}\) fixed and define \(\theta_0\) by replacing every block with the strictly positive uniform table
\[
[\Pi_{\theta_0,y}]_{b,v}=1/u.
\]
Every block map then has one-dimensional image, so the composite block-column map has rank at most \(|\mathcal I_S|<u|\mathcal I_S|=Q_S\).  For
\[
\Pi_{\theta(t),y}=\Pi_{\theta_0,y}+t(\Pi_{\theta_1,y}-\Pi_{\theta_0,y}),
\qquad p_{\theta(t)}=p_{\theta_1}, \tag{10}
\]
row sums remain one, and strict positivity holds for all sufficiently small positive and negative \(t\).  Select a \(Q_S\)-minor nonzero at \(t=1\).  Along (10) its determinant is a univariate polynomial which is nonzero at one and zero at zero.  Its roots are finite, so for some \(\varepsilon>0\) it is nonzero whenever \(0<|t|<\varepsilon\).  This proves the first assertion and constructs the crossing family.

Now let \(u=1\).  Row stochasticity forces every \(\Pi_{\theta,y}\) to be the single column \(\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B_y}\).  A demand vector therefore maps to the block-constant vector \(j\in J_S\) with values \(j_{a,c}\), and it is in the kernel precisely when
\[
j\in N_S(p_\theta)\cap J_S
=H_S^\perp\cap R_S(p_\theta)^\perp\cap J_S. \tag{11}
\]
For a block-constant \(j\), orthogonality to every \(r_c(p_\theta)\) is exactly
\[
\sum_{a:\,(a,c)\in\mathcal I_S}
\left(\sum_{b\in\mathcal B_{(a,c)}}p_\theta(a,b,c)\right)j_{a,c}=0
\quad\text{for every supported }c. \tag{12}
\]
Every coefficient in parentheses is strictly positive.  If only one treatment block is present, (12) forces its \(j_{a,c}\) to be zero.  If two are present, a positive linear combination of the two real numbers is zero exactly when both vanish or they have opposite strict signs.  Thus any rank-deficient positive law produces exactly the sign-feasible nonzero vector in the statement.

Conversely, suppose such a nonzero \(j\in J_S\cap H_S^\perp\) exists.  For a \(c\) with two nonzero opposite-sign values, choose positive block totals
\[
w_{0,c}=|j_{1,c}|,\qquad w_{1,c}=|j_{0,c}|;
\]
then \(w_{0,c}j_{0,c}+w_{1,c}j_{1,c}=0\).  If both values are zero, or if only one treatment block is supported, choose any positive block totals.  Distribute each \(w_{a,c}\) positively across the finitely many cells \(b\in\mathcal B_{(a,c)}\), and normalize all cell weights by their positive grand total.  The resulting \(p_0\) is strictly positive on exactly \(S\), and (12) holds.  Equation (11) then gives a nonzero kernel vector, so the corresponding \(\theta_0\) is rank deficient.

If no sign-feasible nonzero \(j\) exists, the necessity just proved shows that (11) is zero for every positive \(p_\theta\); hence the rank is \(|\mathcal I_S|=Q_S\) at every law.  This proves the equivalence.  It is an exact finite test: \(J_S\cap H_S^\perp\) is the solution space of a rational linear system determined by \(D_S\), and the stated alternatives form a finite union of rational relatively open polyhedral cones, each decidable by exact linear feasibility after fixing its strict sign pattern.

Finally, when a sign-feasible vector exists, let \(p_1\) be the full-rank positive rational specialization supplied by the generic-rank theorem and set
\[
p_t=p_0+t(p_1-p_0).
\]
For sufficiently small positive and negative \(t\), this remains a normalized strictly positive mass function on \(S\).  A full-size minor is nonzero at \(t=1\) and zero at \(t=0\), so the same univariate-polynomial argument used for (10) makes it nonzero for every sufficiently small \(t\ne0\).  This gives the required compatible crossing family in the remaining case.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field and let \((V_i)_{i\in D}\) be a finite family of subspaces.  There are vectors \(v_i\in V_i\), one for every \(i\in D\), which are linearly independent if and only if
\[
\dim\left(\sum_{i\in I}V_i\right)\ge |I|
\quad\text{for every }I\subseteq D.
\]

proposed.statement: After one constant column is separated in every row-stochastic block, let the remaining \(u-1\) contrast columns range independently in \(\overline V_y\). The maximum rank of their images in \(\overline E_S/\overline N_S\) is \(|\mathcal D_S|-\eta(S)\). The maximizing contrast array lies in a nonempty Zariski-open set and has a rational representative; sufficiently small rational perturbation of the uniform row-stochastic blocks realizes it with strictly positive entries.
proposed.justification: This is the early kill test and the mathematical hinge converting local structural zeros into an exact global rank loss.
proposed.gap: Rado characterizes independent representatives from prescribed subspaces, while the fortified problem requires simultaneous subspace choices, repeated latent contrasts, a block-constant quotient, and rational positive realization.
proposed.consumer: The theorem supplies the missing attainment step needed by every support-specific completeness diagnostic in the proposal.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Adds the cited independent-transversal theorem that is the sole classical premise of the rank-attainment argument.

proposed.statement: Given \(S\), \(u\), and the quotient rank oracle, a strongly polynomial submodular-function-minimization algorithm returns \(\kappa_0(S)\), \(\eta(S)\), \(r_{\mathrm{gen}}(S)\), and a maximizing deficient set \(I^*\subseteq\mathcal D_S\) using a number of oracle calls polynomial in \(|\mathcal D_S|\). Each oracle call is an exact rank computation over \(\mathbb F_S\); hence the output is an exact certificate rather than a numerical generic-rank guess.
proposed.justification: The theorem turns exponentially many Hall inequalities into an executable exact certificate with a named obstruction.
proposed.gap: Schrijver supplies oracle submodular minimization and Hirai and Iwamasa handle a narrow independently parameterized block-matrix class; neither constructs the fortified quotient rank oracle.
proposed.consumer: Sensitivity analyses over defended proxy subsets can report the precise support blocks responsible for route failure instead of only a failed matrix-rank check.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Adds the cited strongly polynomial submodular-minimization theorem used by the exact oracle algorithm.
